answer:
1. The animation shows how well a fixed income payment has held its purchasing power against US inflation over past 25-year stretches. It tests whether a payment that never rises would have "kept up" with prices.

2. Frame 1 starts with a single bar chart of consumer prices (CPI-U) from 1947 to August 2006. Its counter reads "0 of 655 kept up" and it has a "first check" line. In frames 2 and 3, the counter settles at 17 of 715 stretches that kept up. A second layer is added for CPI-W, the index Social Security uses, at 21 of 715. In frames 4 to 6, a third layer is added for PCE, an index that starts in 1959. Its figures are 19.2% of stretches kept up and a typical 88.0%. Highlighted teal bands mark the stretches that kept up. Every frame carries the labels "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

3. In the US data, almost no 25-year stretch kept up under the CPI measures. That is 17 of 715 for CPI-U and 21 of 715 for CPI-W. Under PCE it was more often, at 19.2%. The "typical 88.0%" most likely means that in a typical stretch the payment kept about 88% of its original purchasing power, though the image doesn't define it. So a payment that never rises usually lost buying power over a long retirement. How much it lost depends on which inflation measure you use.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that a flat payout tends to lose value over decades. For me at 64, that would mean weighing the option that rises with inflation against the flat one, and the frames don't say which to pick.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows historical data, and its own caption says it is "history, not a forecast." It doesn't mention annuities or recommend either payout option.
